name: Khasian
region: The Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya in northeast India, and adjacent Bangladesh
defining_innovation: Khasi, Pnar and War, an Austroasiatic outpost in northeast India among Tibeto-Burman and Indo-Aryan neighbours, probably closest to the Palaungic languages of Myanmar.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body: The Khasian languages are spoken in the hills of Meghalaya, cut off from other Austroasiatic languages by Tibeto-Burman, Tai and Indo-Aryan speakers. Sidwell and others have proposed that they are closest to the Palaungic languages of northern Myanmar, forming a 'Khasi-Palaungic' group. Khasi has about a million and a half speakers, and it keeps the typical mainland Austroasiatic word order and word structure, unlike Munda.

chapters.title: Writing and Recognition
chapters.body: Khasi was first written systematically by the Welsh Calvinist missionary **Thomas Jones**, who arrived in 1841 and adapted the Latin alphabet to it, using Welsh spelling conventions in places. Mission schools and a Khasi Bible followed, and Khasi developed a lively literature and press. It is an associate official language of Meghalaya. Its speakers have long campaigned for its inclusion in India's Eighth Schedule.

turning_points.title: An outpost in Meghalaya
turning_points.description: The ancestors of the Khasi settle the hills of Meghalaya and separate from their Palaungic relatives to the east. Whether Khasian and Palaungic really form a subgroup is still being tested.

sources.citation: Jenny, Mathias & Paul Sidwell, eds. 2015. The Handbook of Austroasiatic Languages. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: Tibeto-Burman and Indo-Aryan neighbours
turning_points.description: Khasi borrows from Tibeto-Burman neighbours in the northeast and from Bengali and Assamese in the plains below, while keeping its Austroasiatic grammar.

sources.citation: Jenny, Mathias & Paul Sidwell, eds. 2015. The Handbook of Austroasiatic Languages. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: Khasi in Latin letters
turning_points.description: Thomas Jones and the Welsh mission create a Latin orthography for Khasi, and schools, scripture and newspapers in Khasi follow. His role is commemorated in Meghalaya today.

sources.citation: Jenny, Mathias & Paul Sidwell, eds. 2015. The Handbook of Austroasiatic Languages. Leiden: Brill.
